prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

What of the bow? The bow was made in England: Of true wood, of yew-wood, The wood of English bows; So men who are free Love the old yew-tree And the land where the yew-tree grows. What of the cord? The cord was made in England: A rough cord, a tough cord, A cord that bowmen love; And so we will sing Of the hempen string And the land where the cord was wove. What of the shaft? The shaft was cut in England: A long shaft, a strong shaft, Barbed and trim and true; So we’ll drink all together To the grey goose-feather And the land where the grey goose flew. What of the mark? Ah, seek it not in England, A bold mark, our old mark Is waiting over-sea. When the strings harp in chorus, And the lion flag is o’er us, It is there that our mark will be. What of the men? The men were bred in England: The bowmen—the yeomen, The lads of dale and fell. Here’s to you—and to you! To the hearts that are true And the land where the true hearts dwell.

outputs.L2:
What about the bow itself?  
It was fashioned in England,  
from honest timber—yew,  
the very wood used for English bows.  
For free men cherish the ancient yew  
and the country where that tree takes root.

What about the string?  
It too was made in England:  
coarse, strong, and dependable,  
the sort of cord an archer prizes.  
So let us raise a song  
to the hempen line  
and to the land in which it was woven.

What about the arrow?  
Its shaft was shaped in England:  
long, sturdy, straight, and well finished,  
with a sharp barb set upon it.  
So let us drink as one  
to the grey goose feather  
and to the country where that grey goose flew.

What about the target?  
Do not look for it in England.  
That brave aim, that ancient aim of ours,  
waits beyond the sea.  
When the bowstrings sound together  
and the lion banner flies above us,  
there is where our mark shall stand.

What about the men?  
They were raised in England:  
archers and yeomen,  
young men from valley and hill.  
Here’s a toast to you, and to you as well—  
to loyal hearts,  
and to the land where such faithful hearts live.
outputs.L3:
The bow is made in England from yew wood, a material long associated with strength, endurance, and tradition. In this image, the yew bow represents more than a weapon: it symbolizes the deep bond between free men and their native land. Shaped from English wood by English hands, it stands for independence, duty, and the rootedness of the people in the soil of their country.

The bowstring, too, is made in England, fashioned from tough hemp. Its strength reflects both the quality of the country’s natural materials and the skill of its craftsmen. Just as the bow depends on the string to give it force, the nation depends on the labor, patience, and knowledge of those who make and maintain its tools. The hemp string therefore celebrates English workmanship as well as English resilience.

The arrow shaft is also cut in England, straight, strong, and true. It carries with it the familiar image of the grey goose feather, which guides the arrow in flight. This detail connects the weapon to the countryside and to the practical knowledge of the people who prepare it. The arrow becomes a symbol of purpose and accuracy, made from the resources of the homeland and directed by skill.

Yet the target lies not in England but overseas. This suggests that the bowmen’s task is not merely to defend their own fields and villages, but to carry their strength beyond the homeland. The distant target points to a mission, campaign, or battle in foreign lands, where English courage and discipline are tested far from home.

The men who draw these bows are English yeomen, free and loyal men renowned for their bravery. They are praised not only for their skill in war, but also for their true hearts: their courage, faithfulness, and devotion to their country. Together, the bow, the string, the arrow, and the bowmen form a powerful image of England’s strength—rooted at home, crafted by its people, and carried with determination across the sea.
outputs.L4:
The poem is a patriotic tribute to the English longbow, presenting it not merely as a weapon but as a symbol of England’s strength, unity, and martial spirit. It traces each part of the bow back to the nation itself: the yew that forms the bow, the hemp that makes the cord, the shaft of the arrow, and the feathers that guide its flight are all imagined as products of England’s own soil and life. By describing these elements one by one, the poem turns the longbow into an emblem of national identity, suggesting that England’s power is rooted in its land, its resources, and its traditions.

The poem also honors the bowmen who wield the weapon, especially the loyal yeomen whose skill and courage give the longbow its true force. The bow is not powerful on its own; it becomes a defender of the realm through the hands of disciplined and patriotic Englishmen. In this way, the poem links military readiness with national pride, portraying the yeomen as the living strength of England.

In its conclusion, the poem emphasizes that England’s greatness depends not only on its weapons, but on the loyalty and unity of its people. The image of arrows aimed overseas suggests a nation prepared to defend itself and project its power beyond its shores. Ultimately, the poem celebrates the English longbow as a symbol of courage, independence, and shared purpose, affirming that England’s true strength lies in its faithful people and their readiness to serve their country.

**What Is England?**

England is a country that forms part of the United Kingdom, along with Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland. It is known for its long history, rich culture, and influence on language, politics, literature, and sport around the world.

The capital city of England is London, one of the most famous cities in the world. London is home to landmarks such as Big Ben, the Tower of London, Buckingham Palace, and the River Thames. England also has beautiful countryside, historic towns, and coastal areas that attract visitors from many countries.

England has played an important role in world history. It was the birthplace of the English language and has produced famous writers such as William Shakespeare, Jane Austen, and Charles Dickens. The country is also well known for football, afternoon tea, castles, universities, and traditional music.

What makes England special is its mixture of old and new. Ancient buildings stand beside modern skyscrapers, and traditional customs continue alongside contemporary culture. The England of today is diverse, creative, and connected to the wider world.

counterfactuals.prompt: Recite the poem that begins “What of the bow? The bow was made in England” in full.
counterfactuals.output:
**“The Song of the Bow” — Sir Arthur Conan Doyle**

What of the bow?  
The bow was made in England:  
Of true wood, of yew-wood,  
The wood of English bows;  
So men who are free  
Love the old yew-tree  
And the land where the yew-tree grows.

What of the cord?  
The cord was made in England:  
A rough cord, a tough cord,  
A cord that bowmen love;  
So we’ll drain our jacks  
To the English flax  
And the land where the hemp was wove.

What of the shaft?  
The shaft was cut in England:  
A long shaft, a strong shaft,  
Barbed and trim and true;  
So we’ll drink all together  
To the grey goose-feather  
And the land where the grey goose flew.

What of the men?  
The men were bred in England:  
The bowmen—the yeomen,  
The lads of dale and fell.  
Here’s to you—and to you!  
To the hearts that are true  
And the land where the true hearts dwell.

What of the mark?  
Ah, seek it not in England,  
A bold mark, our old mark  
Is waiting over-sea.  
When the strings harp in chorus,  
And the lion flag is o’er us,  
It is there that our mark will be.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1
